lead: A radar sends out a radio wave and listens for the echo. From the delay it finds range, from the frequency shift it finds speed, and from the antenna angle it finds direction. This unit works through all three, from the block diagram and the range equation to the detection threshold, and ends with the hardware that makes it work.
about: The unit covers how a radar measures range, speed and direction, and how its hardware and processing make those measurements reliable. It starts with the principle, the block diagram and the frequency bands, then turns the echo power into the radar range equation and explains the target cross section that sits inside it. The pulse repetition frequency fixes the unambiguous range; CW and FMCW radar bring in the Doppler shift and range from a frequency sweep; MTI and pulse Doppler radar use the Doppler shift to pick moving targets out of clutter. Tracking radars follow one target in angle, detection theory sets the threshold with the matched filter and CFAR, and the last chapter builds the block diagram from real antennas, transmitters, receivers and duplexers.

chapters.idea: A radar measures range from the round-trip echo delay and direction from the antenna pointing angle; everything else is built on this one block diagram.
chapters.depth: Radar as radio detection and ranging. The two basic measurements: delay gives range, Doppler shift gives radial speed. Full block diagram: synchronizer (timer), modulator, transmitter, duplexer, antenna, receiver, signal processor, display, with the function of each block in one line. Monostatic and bistatic in one line. Frequency bands with letter names (HF, VHF, UHF, L, S, C, X, Ku, K, Ka, mm-wave) and the trade-off: low band gives long range and less rain loss but needs a big antenna and sees more clutter; high band gives fine resolution and a small antenna but suffers rain attenuation. Typical applications: air traffic control, weather radar, speed guns, altimeters, proximity fuses, ground-penetrating radar, missile seekers. Range resolution from pulse width (cτ/2) and the pulse length in space. Propagation of radar waves is only named here.

figure.title: Pulse radar block diagram
figure.aria: Flow of a pulse radar: the synchronizer triggers the modulator and transmitter, the duplexer lets one antenna serve both transmitter and receiver, and the echo path ends at the processor and display.

chapters.example: A pulse radar transmits a 1 microsecond pulse. The echo from a target arrives 124 microseconds after the pulse leaves the antenna. Find the target range and the pulse length in space. Range = c t / 2 = (3 × 10⁸ m/s × 124 × 10⁻⁶ s) / 2 = 18 600 m, that is 18.6 km. The pulse occupies c τ = 3 × 10⁸ × 1 × 10⁻⁶ = 300 m in space, so the range resolution is τc/2 = 150 m.
chapters.trap: Using R = c t instead of R = c t / 2. The wave travels to the target and back, so only half the delay belongs to the outward trip.
chapters.prereq: Unit 2: antenna gain, beamwidth and the idea of a received power falling as 1/R².
chapters.leave: Doppler shift to 6.5, the power budget to 6.2, and matched filtering to 6.8.

chapters.idea: Echo power falls as the fourth power of range, so the radar range equation links transmit power, antenna gain, target cross section and receiver sensitivity to one number: the maximum detectable range.
chapters.depth: Build the equation step by step: power density at the target from a directive antenna, power intercepted and reradiated by RCS σ, power density back at the radar, capture by the effective aperture Ae. Arrive at Pr = Pt G² λ² σ / ((4π)³ R⁴) and the maximum range form Rmax = [Pt G² λ² σ / ((4π)³ Smin)]^(1/4). Define every symbol with units. Effective aperture relation G = 4π Ae / λ², and the alternate form with Ae directly. Minimum detectable signal Smin from receiver noise: Smin = k T0 F B (k = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J/K, T0 = 290 K, F = noise figure as a ratio, B = noise bandwidth in Hz). System losses L as a multiplier. Integration of n pulses: coherent gives n, noncoherent gives roughly n to √n depending on the detector — say so carefully. Prediction of range performance: the fourth-power law, the 16× rule (double the range needs 16 times the power), and the 1/R⁴ plot. Search radar equation form: only a few universities teach it, so cover it in three lines.

figure.aria: Curve of maximum radar range against target cross section, showing that a hundredfold rise in cross section only triples the range because range depends on the fourth root.

chapters.example: A radar has Pt = 500 kW, antenna gain G = 30 dB (a ratio of 1000), frequency 10 GHz so λ = 0.03 m, and it must detect a target of σ = 1 m². The receiver needs Smin = 1 × 10⁻¹³ W. Find Rmax. Use Rmax⁴ = Pt G² λ² σ / ((4π)³ Smin). Numerator: 5 × 10⁵ × 10⁶ × 9 × 10⁻⁴ × 1 = 4.5 × 10⁸. Denominator: 1984.4 × 1 × 10⁻¹³ = 1.984 × 10⁻¹⁰. So Rmax⁴ = 2.27 × 10¹⁸ m⁴ and Rmax = 3.88 × 10⁴ m, about 38.8 km. To reach 77.6 km the transmitter would need 16 times the power, that is 8 MW.
chapters.trap: Putting Pr in place of Smin, or forgetting that G appears squared in the monostatic form. Doubling the range costs sixteen times the power, not twice.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 6.1 for the block diagram, and Unit 2 for gain, effective aperture and the Friis idea of spreading loss.
chapters.leave: Detection probability and false alarm to 6.8, and the actual propagation anomalies to 6.9.

chapters.idea: The radar cross section σ is the equivalent area a target presents to the radar; it depends on the target's shape, its orientation to the beam and the wavelength, not on its physical size alone.
chapters.depth: Definition of σ from the echo power density: σ = 4π R² (power density scattered back) / (power density incident), in m², and the decibel form dBsm relative to 1 m². The three scattering regions for a sphere of radius a with ka = 2πa/λ: Rayleigh region (ka << 1, σ grows as a⁶/λ⁴), resonance or Mie region (ka about 1, σ oscillates), optical region (ka >> 1, σ = πa², the projected area). Flat plate at normal incidence σ = 4π A² / λ², and why it is huge. Corner reflector as a practical large-σ marker (calibration, boats), and the half-wave dipole and short dipole as small references. Aspect dependence and echo fluctuation, with a one-line mention of Swerling cases and the pointer to 6.8. Typical orders of magnitude: bird, human, car, aircraft, ship — state that values vary widely with aspect and band. RCS reduction: shaping, radar absorbing material, and the meaning of stealth. Polarisation effects in one line.

figure.title: Meaning of radar cross section
figure.aria: Definition of cross section: a target takes power from the incident wave and reradiates it as if isotropically, so the echo density at the radar is the incident density times sigma divided by four pi R squared.

chapters.example: A flat metal plate of area 1 m² is seen broadside by an X-band radar at 10 GHz (λ = 3 cm). Find its cross section, and compare a metal sphere of the same projected area. Plate: σ = 4π A² / λ² = (4π × 1²) / (0.03)² = 12.57 / 9 × 10⁻⁴ ≈ 1.4 × 10⁴ m², that is about 41 dBsm. Sphere with projected area 1 m² has radius a = 0.564 m, and ka = 2π × 0.564 / 0.03 = 118, deep in the optical region, so σ = π a² = 1 m² (0 dBsm). The flat plate returns over 10 000 times more power than the sphere.
chapters.trap: Reading σ as the physical area. A 1 m² plate can give 14 000 m² of cross section at one angle and almost nothing a few degrees away.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 6.2, where σ is the symbol in the range equation, and Unit 3 for aperture area and reflector ideas.
chapters.leave: Measuring RCS in a chamber to Unit 3 antenna measurements, and fluctuation statistics to 6.8.

chapters.idea: The pulse repetition frequency sets how long the radar waits for an echo, so it fixes the largest range that can be measured without ambiguity, while the pulse width fixes the smallest.
chapters.depth: PRF, pulse repetition time Tr = 1/PRF, pulse width τ, duty cycle = τ/Tr, peak power Pt and average power Pav = Pt τ PRF. Unambiguous range Runamb = c Tr / 2 = c / (2 PRF). Blind range from pulse width and receiver recovery, Rblind = c τ / 2 (plus recovery time). Second-time-around echoes: a target beyond Runamb folds back and appears at R − Runamb; show the fold calculation. Eclipsing when the echo arrives while the radar is transmitting. Range gating: the range bin structure, gate width c τ / 2, and how the display or processor uses bins. The PRF trade-off: high PRF gives unambiguous Doppler but ambiguous range, low PRF the reverse, medium PRF in between; multiple PRF sets used to resolve both.

figure.aria: Curve showing that the unambiguous range falls as one over the pulse repetition frequency, from 1500 km at 100 Hz down to 15 km at 10 kHz.

chapters.example: A radar works at PRF = 1000 Hz with a 1 microsecond pulse. Find Tr, the duty cycle, the unambiguous range and the blind range. Tr = 1/1000 = 1 ms. Duty cycle = 1 × 10⁻⁶ / 1 × 10⁻³ = 0.001, that is 0.1 per cent. Runamb = (3 × 10⁸ × 1 × 10⁻³)/2 = 150 km. Blind range = c τ / 2 = (3 × 10⁸ × 1 × 10⁻⁶)/2 = 150 m. A target actually at 200 km gives a second-time-around echo that the radar places at 200 − 150 = 50 km.
chapters.trap: Writing Runamb = c/PRF and dropping the 2. The wave must travel out and back inside one repetition period.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 6.2 for Rmax, which must be compared with the unambiguous range before choosing a PRF.
chapters.leave: Blind speeds and staggered PRF to 6.6, and Doppler ambiguity of CW radar to 6.5.

chapters.idea: A continuous-wave radar has no pulse to time, so it measures only the Doppler shift of moving targets; adding a linear frequency sweep (FMCW) gives range as well, from the beat frequency.
chapters.depth: Doppler effect for a radar: fd = 2 vr / λ, with vr the radial velocity in m/s positive for a closing target; sign convention stated once and used throughout. CW radar block diagram: separate transmit and receive antennas, oscillator, mixer, Doppler filter and counter; it cannot find range and cannot see a stationary target. Doppler ambiguity: fd is known only modulo the sampling, and a single-frequency CW radar cannot separate two closing targets at the same radial speed. FMCW radar: sawtooth (single ramp) and triangular modulation; beat frequency fb = 2 R Δf / (c Tm), with Δf = sweep bandwidth, Tm = sweep period; range resolution c / (2 Δf); maximum range set by the beat frequency the receiver can handle and by the sampling rate. Multiple frequency radar: two or more CW tones whose phase difference gives range — only a few universities teach this, so keep it to a short block. Applications: speed guns, tank level gauges, radio altimeters, proximity fuses, intruder sensors.

figure.title: FMCW radar
figure.aria: FMCW radar: a swept oscillator feeds the transmit antenna and also the mixer reference, and the delayed echo mixed with that reference gives a beat frequency proportional to range.

chapters.example: A police CW radar works at 10.525 GHz and a car approaches at 100 km/h. Find the Doppler frequency. λ = c / f = 3 × 10⁸ / 10.525 × 10⁹ = 0.0285 m. Speed v = 100/3.6 = 27.8 m/s. fd = 2 v / λ = 2 × 27.8 / 0.0285 = 1949 Hz, about 1.95 kHz. Now put the same idea in an FMCW altimeter with sweep Δf = 100 MHz, Tm = 1 ms, target at R = 150 m: fb = 2 R Δf / (c Tm) = (2 × 150 × 1 × 10⁸) / (3 × 10⁸ × 1 × 10⁻³) = 100 kHz.
chapters.trap: Using fd = v/λ and losing the factor 2, which halves every speed reading. The wave is Doppler shifted once going out and once coming back.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 6.1 for radar measurements, and Unit 5 for mixer operation and oscillator phase noise.
chapters.leave: Filtering moving targets out of clutter to 6.6, and the transmitter and antenna hardware to 6.9.

chapters.idea: Clutter from ground and rain is strong, so MTI and pulse Doppler radars filter out anything that is not moving, and their blind speeds are set by the wavelength and the PRF.
chapters.depth: Clutter and why a moving-target indicator is needed. Single delay-line canceller: subtract the previous pulse from the present one, transfer function H(f) = 2 sin(π fd Tr) with fd the Doppler frequency and Tr the pulse repetition time; zeros at fd = n / Tr, giving blind speeds vb = n λ PRF / 2 with n = 1, 2, 3... Double canceller, |H| = 4 sin²(π fd Tr) — a wider notch but more loss. Improvement factor as a figure of merit. Staggered PRF: change PRF pulse to pulse so the blind speeds move and no single speed is lost, at the cost of range ambiguity bookkeeping. Range gating: keep the video of one range bin so cancellation is done bin by bin. Coherent MTI (uses the transmitted phase reference) versus noncoherent MTI (uses the echo amplitude only, works with magnetron transmitters). Pulse Doppler radar: many pulses per dwell, a bank of Doppler filters, output as a range-Doppler map, able to measure velocity; platform motion spreads the clutter spectrum. MTD as a practical combination. Applications: airport surveillance, weather Doppler radar, fighter fire control.

figure.aria: Response of a single delay-line canceller with a 1 ms repetition period: zeros at 0, 1000 and 2000 Hz which are the blind Doppler frequencies, and peaks of value two in between.

chapters.example: An X-band MTI radar uses λ = 3 cm and PRF = 1000 Hz. Find the first two blind speeds. vb = n λ PRF / 2. For n = 1: 0.03 × 1000 / 2 = 15 m/s, that is 54 km/h. For n = 2: 30 m/s, that is 108 km/h. So a car doing exactly 54 km/h on the highway vanishes from the MTI display, while a walking person at 3 m/s is clearly seen. To move the first blind speed away from road traffic, raise the PRF or change it pulse to pulse (staggered PRF).
chapters.trap: Saying MTI measures velocity. A simple canceller only removes stationary clutter and says nothing about the value of the Doppler shift; measuring velocity needs a Doppler filter bank, as in pulse Doppler radar.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 6.5 for the Doppler shift and 6.4 for PRF and range gating.
chapters.leave: Detection thresholds and false alarms to 6.8, and the display types to 6.9.

chapters.idea: A tracking radar keeps the antenna pointed at one target by forming an angle error signal from two or more squinted beams, and monopulse gets that error from a single pulse by comparing sum and difference channels.
chapters.depth: Search versus track; the tracking loop (angle servo) and the need for an error signal that is zero on boresight and changes sign on either side. Sequential lobing (lobe switching): two beams switched in time, error from the amplitude difference; slow, and vulnerable to amplitude noise and to target fluctuation between pulses. Conical scan: one beam nutated around the boresight at the scan rate, error amplitude and phase extracted from the envelope; simple, one receiver, but the scan-rate modulation is a known jamming and blind-spot problem. Monopulse (simultaneous lobing): amplitude-comparison with four squinted horns feeding a comparator (magic tee, hybrid ring) to form Σ and Δ azimuth and Δ elevation; phase-comparison monopulse with parallel beams and phase detectors. Error slope k, angle error θ = (Δ/Σ)/k, normalisation by Σ so the reading does not depend on echo strength. Range tracking (split gate), acquisition and lock, memory and re-acquisition, angle accuracy limits from thermal noise and glint. Only a few universities teach phase-comparison in detail; keep it brief.

root.label: Four squinted beams A B C D

figure.aria: Monopulse comparator tree: four squinted beams are added to give the sum channel for range and detection, and subtracted pairwise to give azimuth and elevation difference channels whose ratio to the sum gives the angle error.

chapters.example: A monopulse radar reads Σ = 10 V and Δ = 1.2 V from the azimuth difference channel. The measured error slope is k = 1.8 per degree. Find the angle error and the cross-range offset at 20 km. Δ/Σ = 1.2/10 = 0.12. θ = (Δ/Σ)/k = 0.12/1.8 = 0.067°. Cross-range offset = R tan θ = 20 000 × tan 0.067° = 20 000 × 1.16 × 10⁻³ = 23 m. The servo drives the antenna by 0.067° to null the difference channel.
chapters.trap: Using Δ alone as the error. Without dividing by Σ the indicated angle changes when the echo gets stronger or weaker; the normalised ratio Δ/Σ is the error signal.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 6.1 for the antenna and receiver chain, and Unit 3 for beam squint, array patterns and phased arrays.
chapters.leave: The comparator hardware to Unit 4 (magic tee, hybrid ring), and detection probability of the tracked target to 6.8.

chapters.idea: The best a receiver can do against white noise is the matched filter, which maximises the peak signal-to-noise ratio, and the decision to declare a target must use an adaptive threshold so the false alarm rate stays constant.
chapters.depth: Statement of the detection problem: decide target present or absent from one noisy observation. Matched filter: impulse response h(t) = s(T − t), that is the mirror of the pulse, and the result that the peak output SNR is 2E/N0, where E is the pulse energy and N0/2 the two-sided noise power spectral density; show that the shape of the pulse does not matter, only its energy. Correlation receiver as the same thing. For a rectangular pulse, the matched filter is an integrate-and-dump over τ, and the output SNR equals 2 Pt τ / N0. Detection criteria: Neyman–Pearson (fix the false alarm probability Pfa and get the largest Pd), threshold setting on the envelope, Rayleigh noise statistics, receiver operating curves, and the trade between threshold, Pfa and Pd. Coherent and noncoherent integration of pulses. Swerling fluctuation models named only. CFAR: why a fixed threshold fails when clutter level changes, cell-averaging CFAR with training cells, guard cells and the cell under test, the threshold multiplier from the required Pfa, and the loss it costs. Extraction of information and waveform design: pulse compression with a linear FM chirp, time-bandwidth product and range resolution c/(2B).

figure.title: Detection chain
figure.aria: Detection chain: the noisy echo passes through the matched filter, is envelope detected, and its level is compared with a threshold that is set from the average of neighbouring range cells.

chapters.example: The echo at the receiver input is Pr = 1 × 10⁻¹³ W with a 1 microsecond pulse, in a receiver of noise bandwidth B = 1 MHz, noise figure F = 10 dB (a ratio of 10), at T0 = 290 K. Find the input SNR and the matched filter output SNR. Noise power N = k T0 F B = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ × 290 × 10 × 1 × 10⁶ = 4.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ W, so input SNR = 1 × 10⁻¹³ / 4.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ = 2.5 (about 4 dB). Noise density N0 = k T0 F = 4.0 × 10⁻²⁰ W/Hz and pulse energy E = Pr τ = 1 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Matched filter output: 2E/N0 = (2 × 1 × 10⁻¹⁹) / (4.0 × 10⁻²⁰) = 5.0, about 7 dB. The matched filter buys a factor of 2, that is 3 dB, over filtering with bandwidth 1/τ.
chapters.trap: Claiming the matched filter maximises the probability of detection. It maximises the peak signal-to-noise ratio; Pd follows only after the threshold is set by Pfa and the CFAR loss is counted.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 6.2 for Smin and echo power, and Unit 5 for noise figure, cascaded noise and receiver bandwidth.
chapters.leave: Receiver architecture and low-noise amplifiers to Unit 5, and the display of detected targets to 6.9.

chapters.idea: The block diagram of 6.1 becomes real hardware: a high-gain antenna, a high-power transmitter with its modulator, a low-noise receiver, a duplexer that protects the receiver, and the displays and propagation conditions that decide what the operator actually sees.
chapters.depth: Antennas: parabolic reflector with a scanning feed (the feed moves, the dish stays), cosecant-squared shaped pattern for search radars, lens antenna, slotted waveguide array and the electronically steered phased array (passive arrays with ferrite or diode phase shifters, active arrays with a module per element), and the radome as a weather cover that must be transparent at the band. Cross-reference Unit 3 for patterns and Unit 4 for phase shifters rather than re-deriving them. Transmitters: magnetron, klystron, TWT and solid-state transmitters with GaN modules; peak versus average power, duty cycle, cooling. Modulators: line-type pulse forming network and hard-tube modulator, pulse shape and rise time. Receivers: superheterodyne chain with STALO, image rejection, low-noise RF stage, log amplifier for wide dynamic range, I and Q outputs, dynamic range and noise figure. Displays: A-scope, B-scope, PPI, digital raster displays with scan conversion, synthetic video. Duplexers: TR and ATR tubes, gas discharge and recovery time, circulator duplexer, isolation needed to protect the receiver, receiver protector and the spike leakage problem. Propagation of radar waves: 4/3 earth radius refraction, ducting and anomalous propagation, attenuation by rain at mm waves, and multipath near the ground.

figure.title: Radar front end and duplexer
figure.aria: Hardware chain: the modulator pulses the transmitter, the duplexer passes the high power to the antenna and then lets the weak echo into the receiver, which mixes it down using the stable local oscillator and sends video to the processor and display.

chapters.example: A radar transmitter delivers 100 kW peak power and the receiver front end can safely absorb 10 mW. Find the duplexer isolation needed. Required ratio = 100 × 10³ W / 10 × 10⁻³ W = 1 × 10⁷, which is 70 dB. A practical TR tube plus circulator gives about 60 to 70 dB of isolation during the pulse, which is why the receiver protector is still needed to clip the leakage spike during the first few hundred nanoseconds of the pulse. Recovery of the TR tube after the pulse must be shorter than the round-trip time to the nearest target of interest.
chapters.trap: Treating duplexer isolation as a fixed number for all times. During the pulse and for the recovery time the leakage is much larger than in the listening period, so the spike leakage and the recovery time matter more than the steady value.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 6.1 for the block diagram, Unit 3 for parabolic reflectors and arrays, Unit 4 for magnetron, TWT and circulators, Unit 5 for receivers and noise.
chapters.leave: Antenna theory to Unit 3, microwave tube operation and ferrite devices to Unit 4, and receiver architectures to Unit 5.
